summary: Specifies a method for resolving IP addresses to HIPPI-6400 hardware addresses and for emulating IP broadcast in a logical IP subnet. It aims for interoperability with HIPPI-800 equipment. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: This is the newer version of the rules for finding computers and shouting to all of them on a very fast cable. It also works with older equipment.

questions: how does ip work over hippi-6400
what is the mtu for hippi-6400
subtitle: How IP packets and address lookups run over HIPPI-6400, a 6400 Mbit/s switched link also called GSN.

tldr.problem: HIPPI-6400 (Gigabyte System Network) standardized a fast point-to-point link and its switches, but left IP networking largely outside its scope. IP hosts had no agreed way to find each other's hardware addresses or to send a broadcast.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2835 puts IP in IEEE 802.2 LLC/SNAP frames on virtual channel 1 with an MTU of 65280 bytes. It defines HARP, a two-phase address resolution protocol built on ARP and Inverse ARP, and a server that emulates broadcast when the switches cannot.
tldr.outcome: The same rules work for HIPPI-800 and HIPPI-6400 equipment, on networks with or without hardware broadcast. The memo admits that coordinating multiple HARP servers and broadcast servers is left for further study.

today: RFC 2835 is a Proposed Standard from May 2000. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 5494.

sections.title: Why IP Needs Rules on HIPPI-6400
sections.content:
HIPPI-6400, also known as Gigabyte System Network (GSN), is a duplex data channel that moves nearly 6400 megabits per second in each direction. Transfers are cut into micropackets of 32 data bytes and 8 control bytes, and four multiplexed virtual channels keep a large file transfer from locking out interactive traffic. The link delivers data in order and supports link-level and end-to-end checksumming and credit-based flow control.

The ANSI standards define the physical layer (HIPPI-6400-PH) and the switches (HIPPI-6400-SC), but they chose to leave networking issues largely outside their scope. RFC 2835 fills that gap: it specifies how HIPPI-6400 switches act as IP local area networks, how IP addresses are resolved to hardware addresses, and how IP broadcast is emulated. A further goal is interoperability with HIPPI-800 equipment.

There are two kinds of HIPPI-6400-SC switch. Bridging switches must support hardware broadcast. Non-bridging switches need not. The memo is written to work with both.
sections.eli5: HIPPI-6400 is a super fast cable between computers. The cable people did not say how computers should find each other on it, so this memo does.

sections.title: Logical IP Subnets and the HRAL
sections.content:
Like the original ARP, HARP has the scope of a logical IP subnet (LIS). All members of a LIS share the same IP network or subnet address and mask. Several disjoint LISs may run over the same HIPPI-6400 network, and ports in different subnets SHOULD talk through an intermediate IP router even if a direct HIPPI-6400 connection would be possible.

Each station needs a hardware address that is unique in the LIS and a HARP Request Address List (HRAL). The HRAL is an ordered list of at least two addresses that identify the address resolution service. All clients MUST be configured with the same list. By default the first entry is the broadcast address FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF and the second is the standard HARP server address 00:10:3B:FF:FF:E0. Further server addresses are optional. How the list is configured is left to the implementation.
sections.eli5: A subnet is like one classroom. Everybody gets the same cheat sheet that says where to ask first: shout to the whole room, or ask the teacher at the front desk.

sections.title: How IP Packets Are Wrapped
sections.content:
IP datagrams follow the HIPPI-6400-PH packet format and travel on virtual channel 1. The packet length, headers and trailing fill must be a multiple of 32 bytes, so datagrams MUST be padded. The padding is invisible to IP and is not counted in the IP length field.

The HIPPI-6400 header carries D_ULA (the destination port's address), S_ULA (the source port's address) and M_len, which is the length of the IEEE 802 packet plus 8 bytes for the LLC/SNAP header. The LLC/SNAP header follows. It has SSAP and DSAP of 0xAA, a control value of 0x03 (which signals a SNAP header), an organization code of 0x00-00-00 and an Ethertype: 0x0800 (2048) for IP or 0x0806 (2054) for HARP. The whole LLC/SNAP header is fixed at 8 bytes.

Because of the header layout, every IPv4 packet spans at least two micropackets. The first has type header, and later ones have type data.
sections.eli5: Each IP packet goes into an envelope with a to-and-from label and a note saying what kind of mail is inside. The post office only takes envelopes in sizes that fit its 32-byte boxes, so extra blank paper gets added.

sections.title: Hardware Addresses and MTU
sections.content:
A HIPPI-6400 hardware address is a 48-bit Universal LAN MAC Address (ULA) in the IEEE 802.1A format, with the usual U/L bit (1 for locally administered) and I/G bit (1 for group addresses). Every port on a HIPPI-6400-SC LAN MUST be assigned a ULA. The memo assumes the Logical Addressing described in Annex A.2 of HIPPI-6400-SC.

The MTU for HIPPI-6400 LANs SHALL be 65280 bytes. That is the same as for HIPPI-800, so it fits in one 64K buffer. The byte accounting for HIPPI-6400 is a 16-byte HIPPI-6400-PH header, 8 bytes of LLC/SNAP, 65280 bytes of IP packet and 232 bytes of unused expansion room, for a total of 65536 bytes. Virtual channel 1 limits messages to about 128 Kbytes, which is still larger than the MTU.
sections.eli5: Every computer port has its own long serial number, like a name tag. The biggest packet allowed is chosen so it fits neatly in one big box, with a little spare room left over.

sections.title: HARP: Registration and Resolution
sections.content:
Address resolution uses HARP (HIPPI Address Resolution Protocol) and InHARP (Inverse HARP). HARP follows RFC 826 ARP, and InHARP follows Inverse ARP from RFC 2390, apart from the HIPPI-specific packet format. The protocol has two phases.

Registration. A client sends an InHARP_REQUEST to the first HRAL address, the broadcast address. If it sees its own request come back, the network supports broadcast, the broadcast entry stays the authoritative service, and the rest of the list is ignored. If not, the client tries each remaining HRAL address at least once every 5 seconds. A server that answers with an InHARP_REPLY is a HARP server, and the first responsive one in the list is the authoritative one. If a port receives its own request on a non-broadcast network, the port itself is the HARP server and MUST provide broadcast service through the PIBES described below.

Operation. The client sends HARP_REQUESTs to the authoritative address and learns from the HARP_REPLYs. Behaviour is the same on broadcast and non-broadcast switches. A port is the target of a request if its IP address is in the target protocol address field, its ULA is in the target hardware address field, or it is a HARP server.

Clients MUST respond to requests addressed to them, use replies from the authoritative server to refresh their tables, and silently discard messages with an operation code they do not support. On non-broadcast networks a client MUST refresh its server entry at least once every 15 minutes. Table aging is required: a client invalidates an entry after 15 minutes and a server deletes one after 20 minutes. A client MUST revalidate an invalidated entry before sending it non-address-resolution traffic. If the server cannot be reached, the client probes the entry's own hardware address with an InHARP_REQUEST and removes the entry if no reply comes.

The server keeps a table linking IP entries and hardware entries. When an InHARP_REQUEST arrives, it updates timers and creates, moves or links entries as needed, which handles cases such as an IP alias moving to a new interface. Permanent entries, for legacy adapters that use static ARP tables, are never aged.
sections.eli5: When a computer joins, it first shouts, then asks the front desk to write its name in the phone book. Later, when it wants a friend, it asks the desk. Phone book entries go stale after about 15 or 20 minutes, so people check them again.

sections.title: HARP Message Encoding
sections.content:
A HARP message is another kind of IEEE 802 payload. The memo requires two packet formats: the generic Ethernet ARP packet from RFC 826 and the HIPPI-800 HARP format from RFC 2834. The ar$hrd field tells them apart, and a reply SHALL use the format of the request. The HIPPI format uses hardware type 28. The Ethernet format uses 1.

In both formats the protocol type is 2048 and the protocol address length is 4. For HIPPI-6400 addresses the hardware address length is 6, and 10 for HIPPI-800. The ar$op field takes these decimal values: 1 for HARP_REQUEST, 2 for HARP_REPLY, 8 for InHARP_REQUEST, 9 for InHARP_REPLY and 10 for HARP_NAK. In requests the requester fields hold the requester's addresses (or zero if unknown) and the target hardware address is zero when it is what the sender wants to find out. In replies the fields are filled with the answer.

A HARP_NAK is a copy of the HARP_REQUEST with only the operation code changed, and implementations MUST support it. The fields are not swapped.
sections.eli5: The messages are filled-in forms. One form type means please tell me, one means here is the answer, and one means sorry, no such name.

sections.title: Broadcast Emulation with PIBES
sections.content:
HIPPI-6400-SC requires broadcast, but early systems may defer it to a broadcast server. When a port finds that the medium has no broadcast, the HARP server MUST emulate it with an IP broadcast emulation server, the PIBES. The PIBES is an extension of the HARP server and uses its current table as the target list. It accepts a message only if the source address is in the list and the destination is an IP LIS broadcast address, a multicast address or 255.255.255.255. It drops anything else, and forwards valid messages to every address in the list. The memo recommends that the PIBES run on the same port as the HARP server, using the same address.

HIPPI-6400 has no native multicast mapping. IP multicast keeps working if multicast packets are sent the same way as packets to 255.255.255.255.

The cost is bandwidth. With n ports in the LIS, the upper bound on the broadcast rate is the total bandwidth divided by n+1, because each message goes into the server and then out to all n ports. The memo says this suits protocols such as RIP, OSPF and NIS but cannot carry high-bandwidth broadcast, which needs real hardware support. It also notes that the same messages and algorithms can resolve addresses for Scheduled Transfer, provided every port also has IP over HIPPI-6400.
sections.eli5: If the school has no loudspeaker, the front desk gets a copy of your announcement and runs a copy to every classroom. That works for small notices, but not for a giant one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo admits there are known security issues with port impersonation through the address resolution protocols used in the Internet. It adds no special security mechanisms to HARP.

It also says that not all security issues of ARP over HIPPI-6400 were clearly understood at the time, because the HIPPI-6400 specifications were still in flux and the technology was new. Given the hole that ARP already allows, it considers other concerns probably minor.
sections.eli5: Anyone on the network could pretend to be someone else when answering who-is-where questions, and this memo does not stop that.

fields.desc: Organization code 0x00-00-00, so the next two bytes are an Ethertype.
